topics.topic: Cross-record lifecycle and timestamp invariants for imports
questions: Which cross-record and chronological invariants must an import satisfy beyond the listed syntax checks?
Which cross-field states are malformed, such as an active project with an archived instant, an archived project without one, or a superseded pointer without a superseded instant?
What lifecycle and timestamp consistency rules must imported pointer histories satisfy?

quotes: A brought-in record is malformed when: a required value is missing (A02); it names a project, customer or room the file does not hold; an id occurs twice in the file; a status is outside its vocabulary; a pointer's type is not declared or its owner service is not the type's (A22); the versions of a project's pointers of one type are not 1..n, or more than one of them is `published`; an instant cannot be read.
A record the import brings in keeps the instants its source holds: a project's created, last-changed and archived instants, a room's added instant, a pointer's published and superseded instants.
judgement.divergence: One implementation accepts any individually readable status and instant satisfying the listed checks, while another rejects lifecycle-inconsistent or chronologically impossible histories; the owner notices which imports are refused and consumers notice the resulting project and pointer histories.
judgement.why: The listed malformed-record checks do not settle the required relationships among imported statuses, marks and instants.

topics.topic: Enforcement of backup retention when creation or deletion fails
questions: Must expiry deletion run even when creating the new backup fails, and what happens when deletion itself fails?
What process enforces the 30-day deletion deadline when a backup fails or when a backup reaches exactly 30 days between daily runs?

quotes: After a backup is written, Registry deletes every backup older than 30 days (30 × 24 hours by its instant).
A backup that fails leaves no partial file, writes a diagnostic that names the failure and no value (A17), and is tried again at the next 03:00; Registry keeps serving.
An erasure reaches the backups when the last backup holding the erased values is deleted: at most 30 days after the erasure.
judgement.why: Deletion is conditioned on a successful new backup, while the same text unconditionally bounds retention of erased values to 30 days despite backup failures.

topics.topic: Treatment of existing backups after backup-key rotation

Each backup is encrypted with the backup key (A17).

judgement.divergence: One implementation immediately loses the ability to restore backups encrypted under the old key, while another retains old keys or re-encrypts those backups; the owner notices whether retained backups remain restorable after rotation.

topics.topic: Whether the one-day recovery-point bound is guaranteed after backup failure

quotes: A backup that fails leaves no partial file, writes a diagnostic that names the failure and no value (A17), and is tried again at the next 03:00; Registry keeps serving.
Data survives the loss of the store with at most a day of changes lost;
judgement.why: Unbounded consecutive daily failures are allowed while the consequence unconditionally promises a recovery point no more than one day old.

topics.topic: Whether withdrawn pointers may be imported
questions: Must a picked project containing a `withdrawn` pointer be refused, or may that status be imported?
Must an import reject a pointer whose status is `withdrawn`?
Must an import reject a pointer whose source status is `withdrawn`?

quotes: It is never imported `withdrawn`, so it carries no withdrawal facts until it is withdrawn in Registry, which records them as for any pointer (owner, 2026-10-31; codex round-02 T1).

A brought-in record is malformed when: a required value is missing (A02); it names a project, customer or room the file does not hold; an id occurs twice in the file; a status is outside its vocabulary; a pointer's type is not declared or its owner service is not the type's (A22); the versions of a project's pointers of one type are not 1..n, or more than one of them is `published`; an instant cannot be read.
Artifact pointer status: `published`, `superseded`, `withdrawn` (R0-14).
judgement.why: M05 forbids imported withdrawn pointers, while A16 accepts every status inside the vocabulary and that vocabulary includes withdrawn.

topics.topic: Access-version behavior when a session ends
questions: Does ending a session conceptually increment its access version before deletion, or is ending exempt from the version-movement rule while still requiring the stated current version?
Does an accepted end increment a version before deletion, or is ending exempt from the version-increment invariant?

quotes: Ending removes the session's record — its set, active project, pending request and access version.

The owner's actions on a session — granting, revoking, changing or clearing the active project, answering a request, ending the session — state the access version the owner saw; a stale one is refused and nothing changes.
accepted change of x => version(x)' = version(x) + 1
judgement.why: A12 requires every accepted session change, including ending, to produce a next version, while A11 says ending removes the version and the entire record.

topics.topic: Authoritative taxonomy establishing security-review completeness
questions: What authoritative category or threat-model catalogue determines that the review is complete rather than merely complete for the categories someone happened to list?
What authoritative taxonomy determines that no security category is missing from the review?

quotes: Every security category has exactly one outcome below, resting on the decisions it names.
for each category c: outcome(c) in {APPLICABLE, NOT_APPLICABLE}
judgement.divergence: One reviewer treats only the nine listed categories as the complete universe, while another applies a broader threat catalogue and requires additional categories and controls; the owner and security reviewers notice whether omitted threats can pass the review.
judgement.why: The claimed completeness invariant has no defined category universe against which it can be verified.

topics.topic: Backup-location conditions that must be verified at startup
questions: Must startup verify that the backup location exists, is writable and can safely create and delete backup files, or may Registry start and discover failure at 03:00?
Which backup-location conditions are startup failures?

quotes: Registry checks the configuration when it starts and serves nothing until every check passes; a failed check stops the start with a diagnostic that names the failed item and never its value (R0-37).

The store must open for reading and writing and carry the store version of the running release; a store of another version, or one that does not open, fails the start — bringing a store to a new version is a step of the release, not of the start.
A backup that fails leaves no partial file, writes a diagnostic that names the failure and no value (A17), and is tried again at the next 03:00; Registry keeps serving.
judgement.divergence: One implementation refuses startup when the backup location cannot be created, written or cleaned, while another starts and discovers the failure at 03:00; the owner notices whether Registry serves without a usable backup destination.
judgement.why: The startup rules expressly test the store but leave backup-location accessibility and safety checks unspecified.

topics.topic: Distinguishing reused session-identity incarnations in audit history
questions: How are the old and new session incarnations distinguished in audit entries and other references when Kernel reuses the same session identity?
How are audit entries for different incarnations of the same Kernel session identity distinguished?

quotes: Registering the same identity again makes a new session with an empty set.
The identity is Kernel's (R0-53, R0-77); the access is Registry's own record, set by the owner alone (R0-46).
the session and the project for a grant or a revocation;
judgement.divergence: One implementation attributes all audit entries bearing a reused identity to the current session incarnation, while another preserves an incarnation discriminator; the owner notices different audit histories and attribution of old grants and revocations.
judgement.why: The text creates distinct incarnations under one reused identity but gives surviving audit references no fact that distinguishes them.

topics.topic: Evidence verifying encrypted disks and restore-VM isolation
questions: What evidence or automated check establishes disk encryption and VM Agent isolation before the backup and at-rest guarantees are claimed?
Who verifies and records that both locations are on encrypted disks before Registry serves?

quotes: The store and the backup location are on encrypted disks of VM Platform; neither is reachable from VM Agent (R0-48).
Whether backups succeed is the owner's to watch on the host (Explicit exclusions: the host's administration).
judgement.divergence: One deployment accepts the encryption and isolation assertions without evidence, while another blocks release until host checks or recorded evidence establish them; the owner, security reviewer and any affected data subject notice the strength of the at-rest and isolation guarantee.
judgement.why: The text asserts host properties as guarantees but names no actor, evidence or required check that verifies them.

topics.topic: Exact dependency artifact and digest representation locked by a release
questions: What exact artifact and digest must the release lock for each dependency?
Which exact artifact and digest representation must the release name for each installed dependency?

quotes: A release names every dependency it runs with, at an exact version, with its digest: every Python package, direct or transitive, by the digest of its distribution file; the Python version; and the base image of VM Platform's Registry environment by its digest, which fixes the system libraries and the store's engine.
judgement.why: The selected distribution artifact, digest algorithm and canonical digest notation are release-manifest field and encoding contracts for State 6.

topics.topic: Failed-sign-in counting and lockout-window boundaries
questions: Which refused sign-in requests count toward lockout, and are window and lockout endpoints inclusive or exclusive?
At exactly 15 minutes, is the oldest refusal still counted and is the lockout still active?

quotes: Registry counts the refused sign-ins of the last 15 minutes, for the whole instance: Registry tells no callers apart by address (R0-27).
The fifth refusal within 15 minutes starts a lockout of 15 minutes from that refusal.
During the lockout every sign-in is refused — the right credential included — and is not counted; the lockout is not extended.
judgement.divergence: One implementation counts every malformed or missing-credential sign-in and includes attempts exactly at the boundary, while another counts only well-formed wrong credentials and excludes boundary instants; the owner notices different lockout timing and availability.
judgement.why: The refusal conditions and exact time-window boundaries controlling lockout remain open.

topics.topic: Linearization of session ending or access revocation against in-flight actions
questions: What event determines whether an in-flight agent call is before or after an access removal?
What outcomes are permitted when ending races another session action?

quotes: The check is made at every call, a running flow's next step included; a revocation holds from the next call on (R0-46).
Cabinet Kernel ends a session when its agent session ends; the owner may end any session in the owner interface.

The owner's actions on a session — granting, revoking, changing or clearing the active project, answering a request, ending the session — state the access version the owner saw; a stale one is refused and nothing changes.
judgement.divergence: One implementation linearizes an in-flight agent action before a concurrent end, revocation or erasure and accepts it, while another linearizes access removal first and refuses it; the agent, owner and affected record readers notice whether the action takes effect.
judgement.why: The rules require per-call checking but do not define the linearization point or ordering of concurrent session and authorization actions.

topics.topic: Normative ordering of disclosure classes
questions: What is the ordering of the three disclosure classes used to decide whether an answer exceeds a token's ceiling?
What is the normative ordering of the disclosure classes?

quotes: Registry uses Cabinet Kernel's classes `open`, `business_confidential` and `personal_data`.
Every service token names one service; Registry knows from its own release which operations that service may call and the highest disclosure class it may receive (R0-26, R0-27).
An answer that would carry a class above the token's highest is refused whole; Registry never answers part of it (R0-26).
class(answer(op)) <= highest_class(s)
judgement.divergence: One implementation orders `open` below `business_confidential` below `personal_data`, while another cannot infer or chooses a different ordering; services notice which answers their tokens receive or have refused.
judgement.why: The access rule relies on an ordering of disclosure classes that no passage defines.

topics.topic: Point of confirmation-value consumption and failures that preserve it
questions: Does a submission with a missing or wrong owner session, invalid CSRF value, malformed request, or mismatched action consume an otherwise valid confirmation value?
At which check is a confirmation value consumed, and which earlier failures leave it unused?

quotes: It is valid only in that session, for 10 minutes, and is used up by the first submission, whatever its answer; a refused submission needs the step shown again.
Every change in the owner interface carries the CSRF protection bound to its session (R0-29); one from another session or none is refused.
judgement.divergence: One implementation consumes a known confirmation value before session, CSRF and parsing checks, while another consumes it only after those checks establish a valid submission; the owner notices whether an invalid request forces the confirmation step to be repeated.
judgement.why: The text says the first submission consumes the value but does not define when a request becomes that submission.

topics.topic: Precedence of CSRF and confirmation checks within the common refusal order
questions: At what point are CSRF and confirmation values checked, and which refusal wins when authentication, rights, target existence, revision, lifecycle or confirmation also fails?
In what order are session validity, CSRF, confirmation validation and consumption checked against the six A04 stages?

quotes: Every action checks in one order, and the first failure is its answer: (1) the caller's authentication and its right to the operation (A09, A13); (2) for agent authority, the session and its set (A10), whose refusal hides every later failure; (3) that the record named exists; (4) the values given (A02, A08, A22); (5) the stated revision or access version (A12); (6) the record's lifecycle — archived, erased, anonymised, not in the set.
Every change in the owner interface carries the CSRF protection bound to its session (R0-29); one from another session or none is refused.
It is valid only in that session, for 10 minutes, and is used up by the first submission, whatever its answer; a refused submission needs the step shown again.
judgement.divergence: One implementation checks and consumes confirmation before target, revision and lifecycle checks, while another checks it later and may return a different first refusal or preserve the value; the owner notices the refusal and whether confirmation must be repeated.
judgement.why: A04 declares a universal first-failure order without placing A13's CSRF, confirmation binding, expiry and consumption checks within it.

topics.topic: Preserving the audit sequence high-water mark across production restore
questions: How is the global audit high-water mark recovered so new entries do not reuse numbers issued after the backup?
How is the pre-restore high-water sequence preserved so that numbers written after the backup are not reused?

quotes: Sequence numbers are never reused (M09): the next entry after an erasure continues from the last number ever written.
Registry keeps that last number durably, apart from the entries, so neither an erasure nor a restart lowers it.
Restoring production from a backup loses every change made after the backup's instant.
judgement.why: Restoring an older backup loses the later durable high-water mark, while A15 unconditionally forbids reuse of the sequence numbers allocated after that backup.

topics.topic: Representation and mutability of OwnerSession runtime state
questions: Are last activity, CSRF state and pending confirmation values facts of OwnerSession, derived values, or separate runtime records, and can the session's expiry change?
Where are the last owner-request time, CSRF state and outstanding confirmation values represented, and are they facts of OwnerSession?

quotes: The facts listed under a model are all its facts, and the facts a create request supplies are named with it (State 0, "Carried to later states"); a fact that may be absent says so in domain words ("when given").
Facts: its identity, minted by Registry at sign-in ("Identity formats"); written once: the instant it began; its expiry.
An owner request is any request to the owner interface that carries the valid session, whatever its answer; it restarts the 30 minutes.
It is valid only in that session, for 10 minutes, and is used up by the first submission, whatever its answer; a refused submission needs the step shown again.
judgement.why: State 1 declares M11's listed facts exhaustive and written once, while A13 requires mutable activity and one-time confirmation state inside that session.

topics.topic: Revision semantics when anonymisation or erasure removes a record
questions: What does moving the revision mean for a transition whose result has no revision or no record?
What revision behavior applies when an archived project is anonymised or deleted whole?
Does customer erasure increment and retain a revision, or only check the old revision before removing it?

quotes: Every action that moves a Project's or a Customer's revision ("Revisions and times") states the revision it was made against: correcting, archiving and erasing a project; correcting a customer, erasing its contact data, restricting and lifting, ending and resuming the relationship.
accepted and changed(r) => r.revision' = r.revision + 1
name, alias, object, customer link, rooms, revision, the request id of its create and every instant are gone;
the Customer keeps its `customer_ref`, this mark and its instant, and nothing else (R0-06):
judgement.why: A04 requires erasure or anonymisation to produce an incremented post-change revision, while M01 and M04 require the resulting record to have no revision, and whole deletion has no resulting record at all.

topics.topic: Scope and extension of the common failure-check order
questions: Where do all operation-specific refusal checks occur relative to the six declared checks?
Exactly which operations are governed by A04's six-stage order, and which stages are skipped when inapplicable?

quotes: Every action checks in one order, and the first failure is its answer: (1) the caller's authentication and its right to the operation (A09, A13); (2) for agent authority, the session and its set (A10), whose refusal hides every later failure; (3) that the record named exists; (4) the values given (A02, A08, A22); (5) the stated revision or access version (A12); (6) the record's lifecycle — archived, erased, anonymised, not in the set.
Only an action that passes all six may be a repeat that changes nothing (A05).
judgement.divergence: One implementation inserts each operation-specific precondition at a different stage or applies the six stages only to record changes, while another extends the order to every operation; callers notice different first refusal answers and whether later checks or side effects occur.
judgement.why: The declared universal order neither locates several required refusal checks nor explains how inapplicable stages work for reads, sign-in, registration and import operations.

topics.topic: Storage, retrieval and lifecycle of uploaded import files
questions: How does Registry obtain the exact file at confirmation, and when are unconfirmed, expired, consumed or superseded uploads removed?
How long are unconfirmed upload bytes retained, and what happens after session expiry, restart, refusal, successful import or multiple uploads?

quotes: The owner uploads the export file (R0-72) in the owner interface.
The mapping names the file by its digest.

The owner confirms that mapping in the confirmation step (A13 rule 6); the confirmation applies the file of that digest, the picks, names, aliases and Customer values the mapping showed, nothing else.
Confirming a mapping after another file was uploaded applies only the file whose digest the confirmation named.
judgement.divergence: One implementation retains every uploaded file through confirmation and removes it on session expiry or use, while another requires re-upload or retains uploads indefinitely; the owner notices whether confirmation succeeds after another upload or restart, and retained personal data differs.
judgement.why: The rules require later retrieval of exact uploaded content but leave its storage, expiry, replacement and deletion lifecycle open.

topics.topic: Trust and production-data classification of the restore-test instance
questions: What trust category and identity status does the temporary restored copy have, and is it an explicit exception to the one-production-instance and no-production-data-in-tests rules?
What trust-boundary category governs the temporary restore instance?

quotes: Test instances — any other instance (the agent's machine, a rig, a developer laptop). Each holds its own identity space and no production personal data; nothing moves between an instance and production except by an explicit import (R0-34).
The one authoritative production instance runs on the owner's home server, a machine on which no agent runs and to which no agent has administrative access (R0-25).
It is a production instance for the test only: it holds production data under every rule of production, configured with no service token, so no service or agent reaches it.
judgement.why: State 0 says every instance other than the single production instance is a test instance holding no production personal data, while A18 creates another temporary instance containing production data.

(6) the record's lifecycle — archived, erased, anonymised, not in the set.

topics.topic: Whether imported identifiers are globally or per-kind unique
questions: Are identifiers globally unique across all imported model kinds, or unique only within each kind?
Is the same UUID allowed once as a project id and once as a room or pointer id?

A brought-in record is malformed when: a required value is missing (A02); it names a project, customer or room the file does not hold; an id occurs twice in the file; a status is outside its vocabulary; a pointer's type is not declared or its owner service is not the type's (A22); the versions of a project's pointers of one type are not 1..n, or more than one of them is `published`; an instant cannot be read.

Any conflict — a project, room or pointer id production holds, a Registry-minted `customer_ref` production holds — or any malformed record refuses the whole import, and nothing changes (R0-50, R0-79).
judgement.divergence: One implementation treats all identifier kinds as one global namespace and refuses cross-kind equality, while another enforces uniqueness and production conflicts only within each model kind; the owner notices whether the import is accepted.
judgement.why: The exact import refusal condition is open because neither the duplicate-id rule nor the conflict rule defines whether identifier namespaces are global or per kind.
